drapeaux.note: The example instruction “call 15” (and the same phrase in the quiz explanation) is the French emergency medical number, kept as in the French; the French text does not gloss it.

accroche: The founding story of the bystander effect is false. The effect itself is very real.
contenu_vulgarise:
March 1964, in Queens. Kitty Genovese is murdered near her home. Two weeks later, the *New York Times* publishes a famous article: thirty-eight neighbors supposedly saw or heard the attack, and none of them called the police.

The account becomes the symbol of urban indifference, and the starting point of an entire research program on helping others.

## The Story Does Not Hold Up

In 2007, three researchers, Rachel Manning, Mark Levine, and Alan Collins, take up the case in *American Psychologist*, with archives to back them up.

None of the three pillars of the account holds. Nothing establishes that there were thirty-eight witnesses. Nothing establishes that witnesses watched the murder: the attack took place in two stages, largely out of sight. And nothing establishes that they all stayed inactive: at least one person alerted the police, and a female neighbor came down to be with Kitty Genovese.

The authors conclude that the story works better as a modern parable than as historical fact.

## And Yet the Effect Exists

This is where we must avoid the easy countermovement. That the founding anecdote is false does not make the research it set off false.

John Darley and Bibb Latané, struck by the case, set up laboratory experiments starting in 1968. The result is robust and has been reproduced many times: the more witnesses are present, the lower the probability that any given individual will step in.

Two mechanisms combine. Responsibility is diluted: everyone assumes someone else will act. And collective ignorance sets in: everyone scans the others to find out whether the situation is serious, sees people who are not moving, and concludes that it is not.

A third factor is added: fear of looking ridiculous. Stepping in in front of witnesses means risking being wrong in public. Hence the paradox of a crowd that makes each person more cautious, and therefore more passive, as it grows.

## What This Shifts

Two lessons coexist, and they must be held together. A badly reported news item founded a field of research: the origins of a science are not always up to the science. And the effect itself is confirmed elsewhere, independently of its founding story.

Incidentally, the research yields an operational instruction: in a crowd, single someone out. “You, in the blue jacket, call 15” removes the dilution of responsibility by reassigning it to a specific person.

repere.texte: The archives establish neither the presence of thirty-eight witnesses, nor that they watched the murder, nor that they stayed inactive. The story works better as a parable than as fact.

carte.punch: Nothing establishes that Kitty Genovese had thirty-eight witnesses.
carte.idee: The archives confirm neither their number, nor that they saw the murder, nor their inaction: at least one person called the police. But the bystander effect itself has been reproduced in the laboratory: the more witnesses there are, the less each one steps in.

quiz.question: What should we take away from the Kitty Genovese case and the bystander effect?
choix: Both hold: the account of the thirty-eight witnesses and the effect it inspired
The founding anecdote is false, but the effect has been confirmed in the laboratory
The bystander effect was abandoned along with the newspaper account
The effect applies only to big cities, as the 1964 article suggested
quiz.explication: The archives dismantle the account of the thirty-eight passive witnesses, but the research it set off has been verified independently: diffusion of responsibility and collective ignorance have been reproduced many times. A scientific field can thus be solid despite a dubious origin, which is precisely what makes the case interesting.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Manning, Levine, and Collins's 2007 review of the Kitty Genovese case reveal?
choix: That the 38 witnesses did exist but did not all see the murder
That none of the three pillars of the original account holds up against the archives
That the New York Times article had underestimated the real number of witnesses
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that none of the three pillars of the account withstands examination of the archives: neither the number of thirty-eight witnesses, nor the fact that they watched the murder, nor their total inaction, at least one person having alerted the police.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what are the two mechanisms that combine to explain the bystander effect?
choix: Diffusion of responsibility and collective ignorance
Fear of the police and lack of empathy
Collective fatigue and the absence of first aid training
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text identifies two combined mechanisms: diffusion of responsibility, where everyone assumes someone else will act, and collective ignorance, where everyone scans the others and concludes that the situation is not serious.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What practical instruction does research on the bystander effect allow us to formulate, according to the entry?
choix: Flee the scene as soon as a crowd starts to form
Wait for someone else to take the initiative before stepping in
Single out a specific person in the crowd to act
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that singling someone out precisely, such as saying you, in the blue jacket, call 15, removes the diffusion of responsibility by reassigning it to an identified person.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Since when have Darley and Latané been running laboratory experiments on the bystander effect?
choix: Since 1964, the year of Kitty Genovese's murder
Since 2007, the year Manning and his colleagues took up the case
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that Darley and Latané, struck by the case, set up laboratory experiments starting in 1968, four years after the murder and well before the newspaper account was challenged in 2007.
